rv.q: It may be the most unusual thing on the London stage right now and is captivating in its glittering strangeness.
Under all the avant-garde bells and whistles, it unquestionably has a heart – a buoyancy and belief in humanity that’s lacking in the original film.
More than anything though, it’s thanks to the emotional wattage of Smith’s voice that the show really soars.
I am beginning to think this Van Hove bloke couldn't direct a seagull to the coast.
Now recognised as an audacious masterpiece, it was the inspiration for The Second Woman — the 24-hour-epic delivered by Ruth Wilson last year — and it drives this similarl...
Whether the show deserves to long outlive its own opening night is another matter.
The emotions are as murky as the story is scattered and the set (by Jan Versweyveld) is messy.
In fact, it’s hard to know what the point is of any of it.
The characters struggle to make it into two dimensions, let alone three.
The show remains a hot mess, unsalvageable.
Opening Night and its lead take you through a performance like no other.
She really gives something of herself in an emotionally raw turn, and, using that gorgeous powerhouse voice, lends some welcome dramatic heft to Wainwright’s meandering songs.
It’s not the least engaging evening of musical theatre I’ve ever sat through, but it is one of the most baffling wastes of talent.
Wainwright's heart feels insufficiently committed on either aesthetic front.
I've rarely seen a production more determined to confuse and frustrate an audience.
But where Cassavetes artfully constructed Myrtle and built an intriguing blur between what is happening in her head and in the play being rehearsed, the blur here topples into a mess.

In a London auditorium, a work of art is being desecrated. “Opening Night,” John Cassavetes’s understatedly stylish 1977 movie about an actress struggling with midlife ennui, has been reimagined as a musical by the Belgian director Ivo van Hove, and the result is a travesty.
How exciting in theory, then, to have a new musical by Rufus Wainwright, with his dual talent of big tunes and lyrics often so poignantly mundane.
It’s a line destined to backfire on those behind a car crash of a production that not even Smith can avert.
Nothing about this musical works, the script is bad and the music is worse, not even Sheridan Smith can save Opening Night from needing to close tomorrow.
Sorry, but 'tragic' is too kind for this unforgivable waste of audiences' time and money.

cn.t: Smith's magnetic performance can't save van Hove's muddled, unfocused musical adaptation of Cassavetes' film. Critics find Wainwright's score weak and the production bewilderingly incoherent, though a few praise its ambitious experimental staging.
